for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

$$
\eqalign{
		\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab}
	}
$$

We can use the product rule to combine radical expressions. 

For example, let's suppose we want to combine the radicals in the following expression:

$$
\sqrt{5x} \cdot \sqrt{6z}
$$

To combine the radicals, we apply the product rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5x}\cdot \sqrt{6z} & = \\ \sqrt{5x\cdot 6z} & = \\ \sqrt{30xz} & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186185310 :tutorial/content "The product rule for radicals also works for higher-order roots, like the cube root. In the case of the cube root, we have

$$
\sqrt[3]{ab} = \sqrt[3]{a}\cdot \sqrt[3]{b}.
$$

In general,

$$
\sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]{a}\cdot \sqrt[n]{b}.
$$"] [17592186184432 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-59e59f90-35db-5fb8-beec-b86dd49456dc" :question/id #uuid "59e59f90-35db-5fb8-beec-b86dd49456dc"] ["question-59e59f90-35db-5fb8-beec-b86dd49456dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-98299"] ["question-59e59f90-35db-5fb8-beec-b86dd49456dc" :question/problem "Which of the following curves is simple?"] ["question-59e59f90-35db-5fb8-beec-b86dd49456dc" :question/worked-solution "A simple curve is a curve that doesn’t intersect itself anywhere between its endpoints.

["question-0fdadb20-0f32-5fc9-95d6-7a680685f826" :question/math-academy-id "q-109092"] ["question-0fdadb20-0f32-5fc9-95d6-7a680685f826" :question/problem "The probability distribution of the random Given that $\text{E}[X]=2,$ calculate $\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-5].$

| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |"] ["question-0fdadb20-0f32-5fc9-95d6-7a680685f826" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{3}$ and $b=-5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-5] & ={\sqrt{3}}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =3\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=2.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{3}+16\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}-{2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-5] & =3\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0fdadb20-0f32-5fc9-95d6-7a680685f826" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-83693d58-e295-516a-afbd-27422e50c864" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point $P(1,1,1)$ is $\,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.$

point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}-1\,,{e}^{-2t}⟩ & =⟨0,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the components yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}-1=0 \\ {e}^{-2t}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other equation. Therefore,  $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-2t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2{e}^{-2t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point  $P(0,1)$ is

$$

$$"] [17592186120215 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-c82dd6ad-d90c-5d9e-b66f-e13eecfeb208" :answer/id #uuid "c82dd6ad-d90c-5d9e-b66f-e13eecfeb208"] $$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [2t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j]\cdot (2i+2t\,j) & =0 \\ 2t\cdot 2+({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 2t(2+{t}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2t({t}^{2}+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since ${t}^{2}+1>0$ for any $t.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=2(0)\,i+((0)^{2}-1)\,j=-j,\end{aligned}
$$

["question-da548a97-bf75-53d6-96e0-6ed458e117e2" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,-1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =c⟨1,-1⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},6t+4⟩ & =⟨c,-c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}=c \\ 6t+4=-c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2{t}^{2}.$ Substituting $c=2{t}^{2}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+4 & =-2{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+6t+4 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}+3t+2 & =0 \\ (t+2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=-2$ and $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-1)^{3},3(-1)^{2}+4(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},-1⟩, \\ r(-2) & =⟨\frac{2}{3}(-2)^{3},3(-2)^{2}+4(-2)⟩=⟨-\frac{16}{3},4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},-1)$ and $(-\frac{16}{3},4).$"] ["question-da548a97-bf75-53d6-96e0-6ed458e117e2" :question/difficulty find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel."] ["question-3a122c89-2594-51a0-a191-07ea14a78a1b" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16+{t}^{3})\,j \\  & =\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(16+{t}^{3})\,j & =c(i+3{t}^{2}\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 16+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 16 & =2{t}^{3} \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =2\,i+(16+{2}^{3})\,j \\  & =2\,i+24\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(2,24).$"] ["question-3a122c89-2594-51a0-a191-07ea14a78a1b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel."] ["question-400be170-ade2-5e44-a6d0-defdf287f3dd" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j \\  & =(2t-2)\,i+\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j & =c((2t-2)i+\,j) \\ ({t}^{2}-2t+2)\,i+(t-1)\,j & =c(2t-2)i+c\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t+2=c(2t-2) \\ t-1=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we obtain $t-1=c.$ Substituting $c=t-1$ into the first equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t+2 & =(t-1)(2t-2) \\ {t}^{2}-2t+2 & =2{t}^{2}-4t+2 \\ {t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the points corresponding to $t=0$ and $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =({0}^{2}-2(0)+2)\,i+(0-1)\,j=2\,i-\,j, \\ r(2) & =({2}^{2}-2(2)+2)\,i+(2-1)\,j=2\,i+\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(2,-1)$ and $(2,1).$"] ["question-400be170-ade2-5e44-a6d0-defdf287f3dd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] "answer-field-6a04d86c-f58b-56e4-9b48-fe0c31d646d9"] [17592186119945 :knowledge-point/questions "question-400be170-ade2-5e44-a6d0-defdf287f3dd"] [17592186121135 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ parametrized by the vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \langle t+1, \: t^2 +1\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

Differentiating this function, we get

$$
\mathbf f'(t) = \langle 1, \: 2t\rangle.
$$

Evaluating this function and its derivative at $t=0,$ we get the following pair of vectors:

$$
\mathbf f(0)  =  \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle, \qquad \mathbf f'(0)  =  \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle
$$

If we view $\mathbf{f}'(0)$ as a vector attached to the tip of the position vector $\mathbf f(0),$ then it will be tangent to the curve $C,$ as shown below.

![](images/85/854d16c788836f784d739f73063354fa3ca2ad233f03cce53b99e5764449f585.png)

Since $\mathbf f'(0) \neq \mathbf{0},$ it serves as a direction vector for the tangent line to the curve at $\mathbf f(0).$ The equation of this line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u) & =f(0)+u{f}^{′}(0) \\  & =⟨1,1⟩+u⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1+u,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $u \in (-\infty, \infty).$

In general, if a curve $C$ is parametrized by a vector function $\mathbf f(t),$ then the vector $\mathbf f'(t)$ gives a **tangent vector** to $C$ at $\mathbf{f} (t),$ provided that $\mathbf f'(t)\neq \mathbf{0}.$

For a fixed $t$ in the domain of $\mathbf{f}(t),$ the equation of the corresponding tangent line is

$$
\mathbf{R}(u) = \mathbf{f}(t) + u\mathbf{f}'(t), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

Furthermore, the vector $\mathbf f'(t)$ always points in the direction that the curve $C$ is oriented. In our example above, as $t$ increases and passes through the point $(1,1),$ the curve is transversed from left to right, and the direction of the vector $\mathbf{f}'(0)$ is also from left to right."] [17592186120011 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0] [17592186198951 :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$

$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le x-y\le 2\}.$"] [17592186198951 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 2,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{1+(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2}du]dv \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}[u]_{0}^{2}\,dv \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{v}^{2}}\,dv \\  & =2[\operatorname{arctan}⁡v]_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186373916 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$

$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2{x}^{3}-1}{{x}^{5}-2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{2x}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{5}})}{(1-\frac{2}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{0-0}{1-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=0.$"] ["question-223b3e58-bcca-5fb5-a51e-27d487af6492" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-53830319-4c61-59d6-b464-6d52b63f8b1c"] [17592186069229 :question/problem "Simplify $\frac{\sqrt{8{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{50x}}$ given that $x>0.$"] [17592186069229 :question/worked-solution "First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{8{x}^{3}}}{\sqrt{50x}}=\sqrt{\frac{8{x}^{3}}{50x}}=\sqrt{\frac{4{x}^{2}}{25}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{4{x}^{2}}{25}} & = \\ \sqrt{{(\frac{2x}{5})}^{2}} & = \\ |\frac{2x}{5}| & = \\ \frac{|2x|}{|5|} & = \\ \frac{|2|\cdot |x|}{5} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot |x|}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $x>0,$ so we have $|x|=x.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2\cdot |x|}{5} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot x}{5} & = \\ \frac{2x}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186069229 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-d40037db-e219-58c5-9dc7-f0a266a679e8" :answer/id #uuid "d40037db-e219-58c5-9dc7-f0a266a679e8"] ["answer-d40037db-e219-58c5-9dc7-f0a266a679e8" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d40037db-e219-58c5-9dc7-f0a266a679e8" :answer/value "\frac{2{x}^{2}}{5}"] ["answer-23dbda11-5ccf-5052-90ff-4a04744a31b8" :answer/id #uuid "23dbda11-5ccf-5052-90ff-4a04744a31b8"] ["answer-23dbda11-5ccf-5052-90ff-4a04744a31b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-23dbda11-5ccf-5052-90ff-4a04744a31b8" :answer/value "\frac{5{x}^{2}}{2}"] [17592186066552 :answer-field/correct 17592186066554] [17592186066552 :answer-field/choices "answer-d40037db-e219-58c5-9dc7-f0a266a679e8"] [17592186066552 :answer-field/choices "answer-23dbda11-5ccf-5052-90ff-4a04744a31b8"] ["question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23" :question/id #uuid "a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23"] ["question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23" :question/math-academy-id "q-162959"] ["question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23" :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{\frac{36}{121{t}^{2}}}$ given that $t<0.$"] ["question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23" :question/worked-solution "First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{36}{121{t}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{36}}{\sqrt{121{t}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{{6}^{2}}}{\sqrt{121{t}^{2}}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{121{t}^{2}}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{\sqrt{121{t}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{(11t)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{6}{|11t|} & = \\ \frac{6}{|11|\cdot |t|} & = \\ \frac{6}{11\cdot |t|}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $t<0,$ so we have $|t|=-t.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6}{11\cdot |t|} & = \\ \frac{6}{11\cdot (-t)} & = \\ -\frac{6}{11t}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-d917ef30-e7dc-5bfc-871f-18df149530e5" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-d917ef30-e7dc-5bfc-871f-18df149530e5"] [17592186068837 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a2aa05db-1a86-5603-983d-94f822e3df23"] [17592186069998 :tutorial/content "To simplify radical expressions, we can use the quotient rule for radicals, which states 

$$
\dfrac {\sqrt {a}} {\sqrt{b}} = \sqrt{\dfrac a b}.
$$

For example, let's simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{16w^2}{25}}$

First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\dfrac{16w^2}{25}}  = \dfrac {\sqrt{16w^2}} {\color{blue}\sqrt{25}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{16w^2}}{\color{blue}\sqrt{5^2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{16w^2}}{\color{blue}5}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression under the radical as a perfect square and taking its square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{16{w}^{2}}}{5} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{(4w)^{2}}}{5} & = \\ \frac{|4w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{|4|\cdot |w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{4\cdot |w|}{5} & = \\ \frac{4|w|}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186069999 :tutorial/content "The quotient rule for radicals also works for higher-order roots, like the cube root:

$$
\sqrt[3]{ \dfrac a b } = \dfrac{ \sqrt[3]{a} }{ \sqrt[3]{b} }
$$

In general, we have the following result:

$$
\sqrt[n]{ \dfrac a b } = \dfrac{ \sqrt[n]{a} }{ \sqrt[n]{b} }
$$"] [17592186068937 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] [17592186069483 :question/problem "Determine the equation of the line that passes through the points $(2,7)$ and $(3,11).$"] [17592186069483 :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{11-7}{3-2} \\  & =\frac{4}{1} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=4$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y=4x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4x+b \\ 7 & =4(2)+b \\ 7 & =8+b \\ 7-8 & =b \\ -1 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

So the equation of the line is $y=4x-1.$"] [17592186069483 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-97d26e7c-a075-5ed5-a723-528daa017501" :answer/id #uuid Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={9}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=9.
$$

["question-8706edb2-e78b-5b3f-a44f-7250c01b8006" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3)(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}=-1.
$$"] ["question-8706edb2-e78b-5b3f-a44f-7250c01b8006" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-53d0c528-6bbe-5382-9d7c-bfcd745b246c" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

["question-df4de458-1c06-5aa0-8cdd-76f4342f8dfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-158531"] ["question-df4de458-1c06-5aa0-8cdd-76f4342f8dfd" :question/problem "Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$"] ["question-df4de458-1c06-5aa0-8cdd-76f4342f8dfd" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that ${x}_{2}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
7{x}_{2}^{2}\ge 4{x}_{2}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \ge 4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=4(1)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\ge 4.$ 

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no smaller than $4.$ But before we conclude that $4$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=4.$

Notice that when  $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+7{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4(1)+7(0)^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the minimum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $4.$"] ["question-df4de458-1c06-5aa0-8cdd-76f4342f8dfd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-89999399-d3ff-5fdc-bb8f-b862f007ad4a"] [17592186157755 :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=x{e}^{2x}.
$$

According to the method of variation of parameters, which of the following is a suitable ansatz for the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)?$"] [17592186157755 :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude."] [17592186157755 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-2f37a13c-db81-5c51-b1fe-cf49ee77cc51" :question/math-academy-id "q-352901"] ["question-2f37a13c-db81-5c51-b1fe-cf49ee77cc51" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-2f37a13c-db81-5c51-b1fe-cf49ee77cc51" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-x})}^{′}+(u{e}^{-x}) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-x}-u{e}^{-x}+u{e}^{-x} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-x}-\cancel{u{e}^{-x}}+\cancel{u{e}^{-x}} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-x} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int 3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-x} \\  & =\int 3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-x} \\  & ={e}^{-x}\int 3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2f37a13c-db81-5c51-b1fe-cf49ee77cc51" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-81614ff3-0cbe-52bd-8674-7e06ead3791c" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-ca23d1f9-e0ba-5c4f-a4c8-1fb3f4fded3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-337398"] ["question-ca23d1f9-e0ba-5c4f-a4c8-1fb3f4fded3f" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y=3x+1.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-ca23d1f9-e0ba-5c4f-a4c8-1fb3f4fded3f" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{2x})}^{′}-2(u{e}^{2x}) & =3x+1 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x}-2u{e}^{2x} & =3x+1 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}} & =3x+1 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x} & =3x+1 \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}(3x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}(3x+1) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2x}(3x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-2x}(3x+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-2x}(3x+1)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{2x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\int {e}^{-2x}(3x+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ca23d1f9-e0ba-5c4f-a4c8-1fb3f4fded3f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-38566c9c-eb99-5a6b-a9ad-b3ded30c9daa" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-ca23d1f9-e0ba-5c4f-a4c8-1fb3f4fded3f"] ["question-74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c" :question/id #uuid "74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c"] ["question-74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c" :question/math-academy-id "q-337372"] ["question-74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y={e}^{-5x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-2x})}^{′}+2(u{e}^{-2x}) & ={e}^{-5x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x}+2u{e}^{-2x} & ={e}^{-5x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}}+\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}} & ={e}^{-5x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={e}^{-5x} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-2x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{-2x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-74b05c82-78aa-5425-a974-d8adb06f503c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5141fac0-843c-524b-87af-8204b1e1c146" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-a6116c6c-0d2d-5d26-9e6b-b6dd0de87989" :question/math-academy-id "q-337452"] ["question-a6116c6c-0d2d-5d26-9e6b-b6dd0de87989" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y={e}^{-3x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-a6116c6c-0d2d-5d26-9e6b-b6dd0de87989" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =x{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a6116c6c-0d2d-5d26-9e6b-b6dd0de87989" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-920d47b2-3068-590e-abf0-2fae86113747" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-16980bbd-b929-5d3b-bedf-b283c32f0104" :question/math-academy-id "q-337710"] ["question-16980bbd-b929-5d3b-bedf-b283c32f0104" :question/problem "Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y={e}^{3x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}."] ["question-16980bbd-b929-5d3b-bedf-b283c32f0104" :question/worked-solution "To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & ={e}^{3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & ={e}^{3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={e}^{3x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =x{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-16980bbd-b929-5d3b-bedf-b283c32f0104" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6640f59d-5879-5651-93ac-a686a27ed14f" :answer-field/id #uuid Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}.$"] [17592186234323 :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+1}{g(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+x)^{'}}{(g(x)-x)^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1} & ={\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{'}(1)+1}{{g}^{'}(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{'}(x)+1)^{'}}{({g}^{'}(x)-1)^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=1,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{''}(1)}{{g}^{''}(1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{-2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}=-2.$"] [17592186233441 :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}.$  The derivative of this function for $x\in (0,\pi )$ is given by

$$
{y}^{'}=\frac{g(x)\operatorname{sin}x+h(x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x)+h(x).$"] [17592186233441 :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x} \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2})+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{'} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot (2x+6)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}x \\ \frac{{y}^{'}}{y} & =\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =y(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Given that $x\in (0,\pi ),$ then $|\operatorname{sin}x|=\operatorname{sin}x,$ so the fraction $\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}$ simplifies to $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)+h(x)=x+3+{x}^{2}+6x={x}^{2}+7x+3.
$$"] [17592186059519 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 23 = \dfrac 2x$."] [17592186059519 :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 23 = \dfrac 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 32 = \dfrac x2
$$

We can now solve this equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{2} &= \frac{x}{2} \\
2 \cdot \frac{3}{2} &= 2 \cdot \frac{x}{2} \\
2 \cdot \frac{3}{2} &= 2 \cdot \frac{x}{2} \\
x &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186059520 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 1{x+1} = 2$."] [17592186059520 :question/worked-solution "First, we note that $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{x+1} = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x+1}{1} = \dfrac 12
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+1 = \dfrac 12
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + 1 &= \frac{1}{2} \\
x + 1 - 1 &= \frac{1}{2} - 1 \\
x &= -\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186059521 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 1{x-2} = \dfrac 3{5x}$."] [17592186059521 :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and
- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{x-2} = \dfrac 3{5x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac {x-2}{1} = \dfrac{5x}{3}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x-2 = \dfrac{5x}{3}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3 \cdot (x - 2) &= 3 \cdot \frac{5x}{3} \\
3x - 6 &= 5x \\
3x - 5x &= 6 \\
- 2x &= 6 \\
x &= -3
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186059522 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 1{2x-1} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}$."] [17592186059522 :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=\dfrac 12$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero, and
- $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac 1{2x-1} = \dfrac{1}{x+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{2x-1}{1} = \dfrac{x+1}1
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
2x-1 = x+1
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x - 1 &= x + 1 \\
2x - x &= 1 + 1 \\
x &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060371 :question/problem "Solve the equation $-\frac{1}{2x} = \frac{3}{5}$."] [17592186060377 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{x + 1}$."] [17592186060374 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{6}{x - 3} = \frac{2}{x + 6}$."] [17592186060937 :tutorial/content "Remember that to solve a rational equation, such as the one below, we can use cross-multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2}{x} &= \frac{3}{5} \\
5 \cdot 2 &= 3 \cdot x \\
10 &= 3x \\
\frac{10}{3} &= x
\end{aligned}
$$

However, there is also another method that we can use, known as the **flip method,** which involves taking the reciprocal of both sides of an equation. So, when an equation involves two fractions, we can "flip" them as follows:

$$
\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{c}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac ba =\dfrac dc
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

The flip method is useful because it allows us to remove a variable from a denominator. For example, applying the flip method, we have

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}x}=\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}5} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\color{blue}x}{\color{red}2} = \dfrac{\color{red}5}{\color{blue}3}
$$

Now, we can solve the resulting equation using the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \cdot \frac{x}{2} &= 2 \cdot \frac{5}{3} \\
2 \cdot \frac{x}{2} &= 2 \cdot \frac{5}{3} \\
x &= \frac{10}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186092914 :question/problem "What is $\cosh (\ln \sqrt{3})$?"] [17592186316986 :answer-field/correct 17592186316082] [17592186317148 :answer-field/correct 17592186315407] [17592186316959 :answer-field/correct 17592186316383] [17592186093453 :tutorial/content "The **hyperbolic functions** are functions defined using the exponential functions $e^x$ and $e^{-x}.$ As we will see at the end of the lesson, hyperbolic functions are closely related to trigonometric functions. 

The **hyperbolic cosine** (abbreviated and pronounced "cosh") is defined as

$$
\cosh x=  \dfrac12\left(e^x+e^{-x}\right).
$$

The graph of $y=\cosh x$ is shown below.

![](images/28/286e0b946edf5c8a8eb23753aaef79812d7c1e7471ab32f43eda81795fb7f47a.png)

The function $y=\cosh x$ is not a parabola, although it may look like one.

Note the following properties of $y=\cosh x\mathbin{:}$

- Its domain is $x\in (-\infty, \infty).$

- Its range is $y \geq 1.$

- It is an even function.

To evaluate $\cosh x$ at some value, say $x=2,$ we simply substitute our value into the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}2=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2}+{e}^{-2})\approx 3.7622\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186093456 :tutorial/content "Just as we do with trigonometric functions, we can use the basic hyperbolic functions $\sinh x$ and $\cosh x$ to create more hyperbolic functions.

$$

$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le x\le 2,\,0\le x-y\le 2,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & \text{ }\text{ }0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}

where $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le \frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1}.$"] [17592186373937 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le \frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{and}\,v=y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}} & \frac{xy}{\sqrt{{(4-{y}^{2})}^{3}}} \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}=\sqrt{4-{v}^{2}}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u\sqrt{4-{v}^{2}}\cdot {v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u\sqrt{4-{v}^{2}}\cdot {v}^{2}\cdot |\sqrt{4-{v}^{2}}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}(4-{v}^{2})\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}u[{\int }_{-1}^{1}(4{v}^{2}-{v}^{4})\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}u\cdot {[\frac{4}{3}{v}^{3}-\frac{1}{5}{v}^{5}]}_{-1}^{1}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}u\cdot \frac{34}{15}\,du \\  & =\frac{34}{15}{[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{17}{15}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186373958 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

A sphere is decreasing in volume at a rate of $54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ Calculate the rate at which the radius of the sphere is decreasing at the moment when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=3\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi $ and $r=3,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (3)^{2} \\ -54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 36\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the sphere is decreasing at a rate of $1.5\text{ cm/s}$ when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$"} {:db/id 17592186297169 :question/id #uuid "0190ee81-75d1-57db-a7fc-6862e592bd65" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Expression"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}.$  The derivative of this function for $x\in (0,\pi )$ is given by

$$
{y}^{'}=\frac{g(x)\operatorname{sin}x+h(x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x)+h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x} \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2})+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{'} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot (2x+6)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}x \\ \frac{{y}^{'}}{y} & =\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =y(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Given that $x\in (0,\pi ),$ then $|\operatorname{sin}x|=\operatorname{sin}x,$ so the fraction $\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}$ simplifies to $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)+h(x)=x+3+{x}^{2}+6x={x}^{2}+7x+3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048601 :topic/id #uuid "ad9b07fe-9198-5d28-975d-6db81bacb439" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186078603 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078240 :question/worked-solution "First, we let

$$
L={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2+h}-{e}^{2}}{h}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{'}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.
$$

We see that if we let $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $a=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(2) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{2+h}-{e}^{2}}{h}=L.\end{aligned}
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{'}(2).$ 

Computing the derivative, we have
 

$$
{f}^{'}(x)={e}^{x},\,{f}^{'}(2)={e}^{2},
$$

and therefore we conclude tha $L={e}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186078408 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078280 :question/id #uuid "3b5966f8-c23f-5ef1-8e5c-7862a020402d" Her position from the starting point, measured in meters, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| **$t$** | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $9$ | $11$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $14$ | $25$ |

$$

$$

Approximate the velocity ${s}^{'}(t)$ at the point $t=7$ using a central difference approximation with the step size $h=2.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the central difference approximation

$$
{s}^{'}(t)\approx \frac{s(t+h)-s(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 
at the time $t=7$ with step size $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{'}(7) & \approx \frac{s(7+2)-s(7-2)}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{s(9)-s(5)}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{14-4}{4} \\  & =\frac{10}{4} \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the velocity of Anna at the instant of time $t=7$ is $2.5\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186297419 :question/id #uuid "6df32816-aa0b-54c8-8b61-f33f7d8c1d99" :question/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "What is ${\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x},$ the lower bound is $a=4$ and the upper bound is $b=9.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{9-4}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\sqrt{4+\frac{5k}{n}}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233961 :question/id #uuid "e1c2de02-e7ba-528c-a6c7-515072028fea" :question/math-academy-id "q-346206"} {:db/id 17592186234344 :question/id #uuid and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{'}(x)$ | ${f}^{''}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{'}(x)$ | ${g}^{''}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-2$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+1}{g(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+x)^{'}}{(g(x)-x)^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1} & ={\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{'}(1)+1}{{g}^{'}(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{'}(x)+1}{{g}^{'}(x)-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{'}(x)+1)^{'}}{({g}^{'}(x)-1)^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=1,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{''}(x)}{{g}^{''}(x)}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{''}(1)}{{g}^{''}(1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{-2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}=-2.$"} {:db/id 17592186050853 :topic/id #uuid "6c00fb56-453a-5851-b57f-240fff460160" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186100845 :question/problem "Let $f(x)$ be the function defined below. For what value of $k$ is $f(x)$ continuous at $x=-1?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{x-1}, & x<-1 \\ 2x-k, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the definition of $f(x)$, the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\frac{k}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{k}{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{k}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}(2x-k) \\  & =2(-1)-k \\  & =-2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(-1)=-2-k.$ 

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) \\ -2-k & =-\frac{k}{2} \\ -4-2k & =-k \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-4$ removes the discontinuity at $x=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186049713 :topic/id #uuid "0d2ecf90-ccdc-56b7-9726-e90d7669ae2f" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186105845 Limits of a Given Function when Simplification is Required"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Given that $f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. - ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty $
II. - ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x)=\infty $
III. - ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty $" :question/worked-solution "First, let's factor the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{(x+2)(2x-1)}{(x-2)(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is  $x\ne \pm 2,$ and we notice that the function can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=-\frac{2x-1}{x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we see that the function has the only vertical asymptote $x=2.$ So statement II is false.

To find  ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=2$ from the left and right.

| $x$ | $1.99$ | $1.999$ | $2$ | $2.001$ | $2.01$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $298$ | $2\,998$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $-3\,002$ | $-302$ |

All values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to 2$ from the left and all values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to 2$ from the right . Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty \,{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=\infty 
$$

Consequently, statement I is true and III is false.

In conclusion, only statement I is correct. A plot of the function is shown below.

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find all of the points where the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+4x+3}$ has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes." :question/worked-solution "To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expressions in the numerator and denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+4x+3} \\  & =\frac{x(x+3)}{(x+1)(x+3)} \\  & =\frac{x\cancel{(x+3)}}{(x+1)\cancel{(x+3)}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

$$
x+1=0\,⟹\,x=-1
$$

Therefore, the function has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=-1$ only."} {:db/id 17592186129092 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128906 :question/id #uuid "83f4e413-e2f4-53dd-9893-fdf8e2df2642" :question/math-academy-id "e-3588"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4317f5b8-cc60-5695-b5bb-47744cecc4cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129633 :question/id #uuid "e0e8d7b9-750d-5053-9cfe-e5211a2c2e3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-38219"} {:db/id 17592186129661 :question/id #uuid "a7ec8526-7c03-5480-8d03-a5cda5bfb1ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-38556"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Infinite Discontinuities of a Piecewise Function"} {:db/id 17592186128906 :question/id #uuid "83f4e413-e2f4-53dd-9893-fdf8e2df2642" :question/math-academy-id "e-3588"} {:db/id 17592186049534} {:db/id 17592186129633 :question/id #uuid "e0e8d7b9-750d-5053-9cfe-e5211a2c2e3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-38219"} {:db/id 17592186129661 :question/id #uuid "a7ec8526-7c03-5480-8d03-a5cda5bfb1ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-38556"} {:db/id 17592186049506 :topic/difficulty 1.1081057366958396 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428973 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x, & x\le 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}x, & x>0.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function?

I. - $[-2,-1]$
II. - $[-1,1]$
III. - $(0,1]$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

So, let's check whether the function is continuous on each of the intervals.

- First, consider $[-2,-1].$ In this interval, $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}x$ and so $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-2,-1].$  Therefore, the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

- Now, consider the interval $[-1,1].$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\operatorname{ln}x)=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)$ has an essential discontinuity at $x=0.$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous on the interval $[-1,1],$ and the extreme value theorem is not applicable on this interval.

- Finally, we note that the interval $(0,1]$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186266042 :question/id #uuid "d91387a3-da34-5d28-af8d-36338cffabf0" :question/math-academy-id "q-131066"} {:db/id 17592186266043 17592186048304 :topic/id #uuid "92d07a33-6647-5dd0-9be4-64be21e6041d" :topic/math-academy-id 3950} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186193530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193827 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to use Riemann sums to approximate definite integrals of *composite* functions. As we'll see, this has some interesting applications.

For example, suppose $f(x)$ is a positive, continuous function. Some values for $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [1,5]$ are given by the following table:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Let's use this data to approximate the following integral:

$$
\int_{1}^{5} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

To approximate this definite integral, we first define a new function $g(x)$ as

$$
g(x) = x^2\cdot f(x)
$$

Now, our task is to approximate

$$
\int_{1}^{5} g(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Let's approximate this integral using a left Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals.

The (regular) step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{5-1}{4} = 1
$$

We can approximate this integral using a left Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals and step size $\Delta x$ as follows:

$$
\int_{1}^{5} g(x) \,\textrm{d}x \approx (g(1) + g(2) + g(3) + g(4)) \cdot \Delta x
$$

Let's add a row to our table with values of $g(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| $g(x) = x^2 \cdot f(x)$ | $3$ | $8$ | $9$ | $16$ | $50$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \int_{1}^{5}g(x)dx \\
&\approx (3 + 8 + 9 + 16) \cdot 1 \\
&= 36 \cdot 1 \\
&= 36
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now look at an example involving a right Riemann sum." :tutorial/id #uuid "c2502b79-d3d8-53e4-be62-b01752a16be9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6553 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "b9769694-1018-5682-8dd1-facf2627a6f4" :step/math-academy-id 39706 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193695}} {:db/id 17592186193547 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193831 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to use Riemann sums to approximate areas under curves of composite functions. Our final task is determining whether these approximations overestimate or underestimate the true areas.

We start by considering *right* Riemann sums. Recall the following facts:

- If a function is strictly *increasing*, the right Riemann sum *overestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.
- If a function is strictly *decreasing*, the right Riemann sum *underestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.

Let $f(x)$ be positive and strictly increasing for $x \in [1,2]$, and differentiable for $x \in (1,2)$. Now, consider the function

$$
g(x) = x^2 \cdot f(x)
$$

Suppose we use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve $y = g(x)$ over $x\in [1,2]$. Does the right Riemann sum overestimate or underestimate the true area?

We note the following:

- Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we have $f'(x) \gt 0$.
- Differentiating our expression for $g(x)$ using the product rule, we get
$g^{′}(x)|= (x^{2})^{′} \cdot f(x) + x^{2} \cdot f^{′}(x); = 2x \cdot f(x) + x^{2} \cdot f^{′}(x)$.
We now examine the sign of each factor in this expression to determine the sign of $g'(x)$.Since $f(x)$ is positive and strictly increasing over the interval $(1,2)$, we have
$2x \gt 0, \qquad f(x) \gt 0, \qquad x^2 \gt 0, \qquad f'(x) \gt 0$.
Hence, we obtain
$g'(x) = \underbrace{2x}_{\gt 0} \cdot \underbrace{f(x)}_{\gt 0} + \underbrace{x^2}_{> 0} \cdot \underbrace{f'(x)}_{\gt 0} = \underbrace{2x \cdot f(x)}_{\gt 0} + \underbrace{x^2 \cdot f'(x)}_{\gt 0} \gt 0$.

Therefore, since $g'(x) \gt 0$, the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing. Therefore, the right Riemann sum *overestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.

Let's now look at an example involving a left Riemann sum." :tutorial/id #uuid "4017a527-6912-5d2d-a92d-3424c1399d67" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6582 :tutorial/title "Determining Overestimates and Underestimates"} :step/id #uuid "6cc57411-9166-578d-ad5d-18fd5906fee2" :step/math-academy-id 39707 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193533}} {:db/id 17592186193694 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193904 :tutorial/content "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines $x=a$ and $x=b$, as shown in the picture below.

![](images/59/59f9a4f76889bf4323c7bcf7dad2dd5269698d94f294458eafdd4c5da0fa0580.png)

When we rotate this region $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis (called the **axis of revolution**), we get a **solid of revolution,** as shown below.

![](images/fc/fc2858aac81addf1d5c19cd3836361d42de4ce844117ab4d42960e45a274026d.png)

It can be shown that the volume $V$ of this solid of revolution is given by the formula

$$
V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} y^2 \:\textrm{d}x = \pi \int_{a}^{b} \left[ f(x) \right]^2 \:\textrm{d}x
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "169b0392-4eed-5202-921f-c379f4264c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7613 :tutorial/title "Volumes of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "5ed00cb2-4d94-5a81-8e1c-488592b9d60c" :step/math-academy-id 44209 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193546}} {:db/id 17592186193695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193905 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$.

![](images/e7/e7fb3f6e11e0e2b51fc4ecae9827a4e378a7981450775f2b9330057c319688bf.png)

The length of the curve between these two points is known as the **arc length** of the curve.

It can be shown that the arc length is given by the formula

$$
L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1+\left[f'(x)\right]^2}\,\mathrm{d} x
$$

where $f'(x)$ is the derivative of $f(x)$.

We can use Riemann sums to approximate arc lengths. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c4aa50-1ce8-52f8-aa97-b2bce6c85623" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7614 :tutorial/title "Arc Length"} :step/id #uuid "4da87fab-f669-5510-93d3-55fea59cbf65" :step/math-academy-id 44210 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193532}}] :activity/title "Approximating Areas Under Graphs of Composite Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186192870} {:db/id 17592186193530 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193827 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to use Riemann sums to approximate definite integrals of *composite* functions. As we'll see, this has some interesting applications.

For example, suppose $f(x)$ is a positive, continuous function. Some values for $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [1,5]$ are given by the following table:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |

Let's use this data to approximate the following integral:

$$
\int_{1}^{5} x^2 \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

To approximate this definite integral, we first define a new function $g(x)$ as

$$
g(x) = x^2\cdot f(x)
$$

Now, our task is to approximate

$$
\int_{1}^{5} g(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

Let's approximate this integral using a left Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals.

The (regular) step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{5-1}{4} = 1
$$

We can approximate this integral using a left Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals and step size $\Delta x$ as follows:

$$
\int_{1}^{5} g(x) \,\textrm{d}x \approx (g(1) + g(2) + g(3) + g(4)) \cdot \Delta x
$$

Let's add a row to our table with values of $g(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| $g(x) = x^2 \cdot f(x)$ | $3$ | $8$ | $9$ | $16$ | $50$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \int_{1}^{5}g(x)dx \\
&\approx (3 + 8 + 9 + 16) \cdot 1 \\
&= 36 \cdot 1 \\
&= 36
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now look at an example involving a right Riemann sum." :tutorial/id #uuid "c2502b79-d3d8-53e4-be62-b01752a16be9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6553 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1997ebaf-5bad-5fd7-875b-27650eb3f5b6" :step/math-academy-id 39566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193531}} {:db/id 17592186193827 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to use Riemann sums to approximate definite integrals of *composite* functions. ![](images/59/59f9a4f76889bf4323c7bcf7dad2dd5269698d94f294458eafdd4c5da0fa0580.png)

When we rotate this region $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis (called the **axis of revolution**), we get a **solid of revolution,** as shown below.

![](images/fc/fc2858aac81addf1d5c19cd3836361d42de4ce844117ab4d42960e45a274026d.png)

It can be shown that the volume $V$ of this solid of revolution is given by the formula

$$
V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} y^2 \:\textrm{d}x = \pi \int_{a}^{b} \left[ f(x) \right]^2 \:\textrm{d}x
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "169b0392-4eed-5202-921f-c379f4264c6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7613 :tutorial/title "Volumes of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "5ed00cb2-4d94-5a81-8e1c-488592b9d60c" :step/math-academy-id 44209 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193546}} {:db/id 17592186193532 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192409 :question/id #uuid "c32c93a7-189d-5dc5-94a4-943ac5bbf29a" :question/math-academy-id "e-10485"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "34555306-3c72-55ef-a59f-ab8d97ae4919" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193025} {:db/id 17592186193069}] :knowledge-point/title "Approximating Arc Length"} :step/id #uuid "7001e0a2-bc0e-5f22-adfb-6688e2d5c0c7" :step/math-academy-id 39568 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193547}} {:db/id 17592186193547 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193831 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to use Riemann sums to approximate areas under curves of composite functions. Our final task is determining whether these approximations overestimate or underestimate the true areas.

We start by considering *right* Riemann sums. Recall the following facts:

- If a function is strictly *increasing*, the right Riemann sum *overestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.
- If a function is strictly *decreasing*, the right Riemann sum *underestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.

Let $f(x)$ be positive and strictly increasing for $x \in [1,2]$, and differentiable for $x \in (1,2)$. Now, consider the function

$$
g(x) = x^2 \cdot f(x)
$$

Suppose we use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve $y = g(x)$ over $x\in [1,2]$. Does the right Riemann sum overestimate or underestimate the true area?

We note the following:

- Since $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, we have $f'(x) \gt 0$.
- Differentiating our expression for $g(x)$ using the product rule, we get
$g^{′}(x)|= (x^{2})^{′} \cdot f(x) + x^{2} \cdot f^{′}(x); = 2x \cdot f(x) + x^{2} \cdot f^{′}(x)$.
We now examine the sign of each factor in this expression to determine the sign of $g'(x)$.Since $f(x)$ is positive and strictly increasing over the interval $(1,2)$, we have
$2x \gt 0, \qquad f(x) \gt 0, \qquad x^2 \gt 0, \qquad f'(x) \gt 0$.
Hence, we obtain
$g'(x) = \underbrace{2x}_{\gt 0} \cdot \underbrace{f(x)}_{\gt 0} + \underbrace{x^2}_{> 0} \cdot \underbrace{f'(x)}_{\gt 0} = \underbrace{2x \cdot f(x)}_{\gt 0} + \underbrace{x^2 \cdot f'(x)}_{\gt 0} \gt 0$.

Therefore, since $g'(x) \gt 0$, the function $g(x)$ is strictly increasing. Therefore, the right Riemann sum *overestimates* the area under the curve $y = g(x)$.

Let's now look at an example involving a left Riemann sum." :tutorial/id #uuid "4017a527-6912-5d2d-a92d-3424c1399d67" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6582 :tutorial/title "Determining Overestimates and Underestimates"} :step/id #uuid "6cc57411-9166-578d-ad5d-18fd5906fee2" :step/math-academy-id 39707 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193533}} {:db/id 17592186193533 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192702 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192410 :question/id #uuid "dbd945a6-786d-515e-8ecd-351dcf6b29f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-10486"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a9946876-7435-589a-a18d-c89c3d790754" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048813} {:db/id 17592186050438}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193027} {:db/id 17592186193028}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether a Riemann Sum Gives an Overestimate or an Underestimate"} :step/id #uuid "d04db767-8034-5d9f-8871-0fb87a4da642" :step/math-academy-id 39569} {:db/id 17592186193546 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192712 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192420 :question/id #uuid "54c6bc65-515f-52dd-8c37-ef6742464361" :question/math-academy-id "e-10520"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea7448d8-a235-52f4-a475-006943f8a142" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193022} {:db/id 17592186193068}] :knowledge-point/title "Approximating Volumes of Revolution"} :step/id #uuid "b9769694-1018-5682-8dd1-facf2627a6f4" :step/math-academy-id 39706 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193695}} {:db/id 17592186193695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193905 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$.
